title: Pushing and Birth
learningGoals: Know what the second stage feels like and how long it can take
Understand different ways and positions to push
Know what crowning is and how care teams help protect the perineum
Know what to do if birth happens before you reach care

review.notes: Clinically reviewed 2026-10-17 by Bryan Kurtz MD, FACOG; every source confirmed against its slides. Pushing with an epidural now presents both resting first and pushing right away. Urge-guided and coached pushing, and longer pushing with a first baby or an epidural, confirmed against CPG 8 and CO 766. Practice Bulletin 198 is kept alongside AAFP for tears. The fast-birth safety slide cites Lamaze; "call 911" and "pull over if driving" are BabyReady's own safety guidance. Updated 2026-10-18: the title slide's label was standardized to the module name; no clinical content changed.

slides.heading: Pushing and Birth
onScreen: Module 2: Labor Basics and When to Call
slides.narration: Welcome back. You've made it through the first stage, and your cervix is fully open. Now comes the part many people wonder about most: pushing, and the moment your baby is born. Let's walk through what it feels like, the choices you'll have, and how your care team helps along the way.

visual.description: Soft, modest scene of a laboring person on their side, a support person holding their hand, a nurse nearby with a warm cloth.

slides.heading: What the second stage feels like
onScreen: Strong pressure low in your pelvis
Often feels like needing to have a bowel movement
Many people feel a powerful urge to push
Sometimes there's a short lull first
slides.narration: Once your cervix is fully open, your baby begins moving down through your pelvis. Most people feel strong pressure low down, often a lot like needing to have a bowel movement. That's normal, and it's a sign your baby is moving in the right direction. Many people feel a powerful, natural urge to push. Some get a short break first, a lull where contractions ease for a bit. If you have an epidural, you may feel less of the urge. Your care team will guide you on when to start pushing. Some suggest resting first to let your baby move down, others pushing right away.

visual.description: Simple side-view diagram of baby's head moving down through the pelvis, with a gentle arrow showing direction.

question.prompt: During pushing, you feel intense pressure, like you need to have a bowel movement. What does that usually mean?
options: Your baby is moving down, which is exactly what should happen
question.explanation: That pressure is your baby moving down through your pelvis. It's a normal, expected part of pushing. And if you do pass a little stool, your team handles it quickly and quietly. It happens all the time.

slides.heading: How you'll push
onScreen: Push with your contractions, rest between them
Follow your body's urge, or
Follow your care team's guidance
Both approaches work
slides.narration: Pushing happens with your contractions. When one builds, you push. When it fades, you rest. There are two common approaches. One is to follow your body's urge, pushing when and how hard it tells you to. The other is guided pushing, where your nurse or provider coaches you through each push. That's especially helpful with an epidural, when the urge is harder to feel. Both approaches work. Your care team will help you find what's effective for you.

visual.description: Nurse at bedside speaking encouragingly, laboring person in a semi-sitting position, partner supporting one leg.

slides.heading: Positions for pushing
onScreen: On your side
Hands and knees
Supported squat, or with a squat bar
Semi-sitting, leaning back
slides.narration: You don't have to push lying flat on your back. Many positions can work, and changing positions can help. You might push on your side, on your hands and knees, in a supported squat or using a squat bar, or semi-sitting and leaning back. If you have an epidural, some upright positions are harder, but side-lying and semi-sitting are still great options. Ask your care team which positions they support, and don't be shy about trying a new one if things feel stuck.

visual.description: Four modest line drawings in a row: side-lying with top leg supported, hands and knees, squat with bar, semi-sitting.

slides.heading: How long pushing takes
onScreen: Anywhere from a few minutes to a few hours
Often longer with a first baby
Often longer with an epidural
Your team watches you and your baby throughout
slides.narration: Pushing can take anywhere from a few minutes to a few hours. It's often longer with a first baby, and often longer with an epidural. A long second stage is not a sign that you're doing it wrong. Each push moves your baby a little, even when it doesn't feel like it. Throughout, your care team keeps checking on you and your baby's heart rate, and they'll talk with you about options if progress slows.

visual.description: Simple bar showing a range from 'minutes' to 'a few hours', with small notes 'first baby' and 'epidural' toward the longer end.

slides.heading: Crowning
onScreen: Your baby's head stays visible at the opening
Intense stretching or burning is common
You may be asked to push gently or breathe
Warm compresses can help protect the perineum
slides.narration: As your baby's head reaches the vaginal opening and stays visible between contractions, that's called crowning. Many people feel intense stretching or burning. It's brief, and it means your baby is almost here. Your provider may ask you to push gently, or to stop pushing and breathe, so your baby's head comes out slowly and the tissue has time to stretch. Warm compresses and gentle perineal massage during this stage can lower the risk of more serious tears.

visual.description: Non-graphic illustration: provider holding a warm cloth, laboring person breathing slowly, support person close by saying 'almost there'.

slides.heading: Tearing and episiotomy
onScreen: Some tearing is common, especially with a first baby
Most tears are small and heal well
An episiotomy (a small cut) is only done when needed
Ask about perineal massage in late pregnancy
slides.narration: Many people worry about tearing, so let's talk about it honestly. Some tearing is common, especially with a first vaginal birth. Most tears are small. They involve only skin or shallow muscle, and they heal well, sometimes with a few stitches. More serious tears are much less common. An episiotomy is a small cut your provider can make to widen the opening. It used to be routine, but today it's only done when there's a specific reason. And here's something you can do now: ask your care team about perineal massage in the last weeks of pregnancy, which can reduce tearing for some first-time parents.

visual.description: Three reassuring icons: a check mark (most tears are small), a bandage (heal well), a calendar (ask about late-pregnancy perineal massage).

slides.heading: Pushing positions, demonstrated
onScreen: Try these with your support person at home
slides.narration: Let's watch a short demonstration of pushing positions you can practice ahead of time.

video.brief: Clothed demonstration with a childbirth educator, a pregnant person, and a partner: side-lying with leg support, hands and knees, supported squat, semi-sitting with partner holding a leg. Shows how a partner can help in each. Notes which work with an epidural. No birth footage.

slides.heading: Your baby is born
onScreen: First the head, then the shoulders turn and slip out
The rest of the body follows quickly
If baby is doing well, they go right onto your chest
Your baby may look a bit blue and be covered in a creamy coating at first
slides.narration: Once your baby's head is born, the shoulders turn and slip out, and the rest of the body follows quickly. If your baby is doing well, they can be placed right onto your bare chest, dried off, and covered with a warm blanket. Don't be surprised by how your baby looks at first. Your baby may look a bit blue and be covered in a creamy coating at first. In the next lesson, we'll talk about that first precious hour together.

visual.description: Newborn on parent's chest, skin to skin, under a warm blanket, parent's hand on baby's back, partner leaning in.

slides.heading: Support person: how to help with pushing
onScreen: Short, steady encouragement goes a long way
slides.narration: Support people, pushing is hard, focused work, and you can make a real difference. Offer short, steady encouragement. Give sips of water and a cool cloth between contractions. Help hold a leg or support a position if asked. Tell them about progress, if they want to know. And stay close. Your presence matters more than finding perfect words.
rows: "You're doing it. Each push is working."
Long speeches or lots of questions
Sips of water, a cool cloth
Leaving the room for long stretches
Holding a leg or hand when asked
Sharing progress, if they want it

visual.description: Two-column table of helpful and less helpful support.

slides.heading: If birth happens before you reach care
onScreen: Call 911; the dispatcher will guide you
If driving, pull over safely
Don't try to slow or hold the baby back
Put baby skin to skin and keep both of you warm
Don't pull on the cord; wait for help
slides.narration: Very fast births are uncommon, but it's good to know what to do. If birth seems to be happening before you can reach your care team, call 911. The dispatcher will talk you through it. If you're driving, pull over somewhere safe. Don't try to hold your baby back. Once your baby is born, put them skin to skin on the parent's chest, dry them, and cover you both with a blanket or towel to keep warm. Don't pull on the umbilical cord. Wait for emergency help to arrive.

slides.heading: Your pushing preferences
onScreen: Positions you'd like to try
How you'd like to be encouraged
Would you like a mirror, or to touch baby's head?
Questions about tearing or perineal massage
slides.narration: Let's add your pushing preferences to your Birth Readiness Brief. Note the positions you'd like to try, how you'd like to be encouraged, whether you'd like a mirror or to reach down and touch your baby's head as they crown, and any questions you want to ask your care team about tearing or perineal massage.
slides.prompt: Write positions to try, how you'd like to be encouraged, whether you'd like a mirror or to touch baby's head, and questions for your care team.

slides.heading: What we covered
onScreen: Pressure and an urge to push are normal
Push with contractions; urge-guided or coached both work
Many positions can work; try changing
Crowning is brief; slow is good
Most tears are small and heal well
slides.narration: Let's recap. Strong pressure and an urge to push are normal signs your baby is moving down. You'll push with your contractions, either following your body or with coaching, and both work. Many positions can help, so don't hesitate to change. Crowning is intense but brief, and going slowly helps protect your body. And while some tearing is common, most tears are small and heal well. Next, a few review questions.

reviewQuiz.prompt: Which statement about pushing positions is true?
options: You must push lying flat on your back
Many positions can work, and changing positions can help
reviewQuiz.explanation: Side-lying, hands and knees, squatting, and semi-sitting can all work. Ask your care team which ones they support.

reviewQuiz.prompt: Why might your provider ask you to push gently or breathe as your baby crowns?
options: To slow things down so the tissue can stretch
So you can rest for an hour
reviewQuiz.explanation: Letting the head come out slowly gives tissue time to stretch, which can help reduce tearing.

options: It's done for every vaginal birth
It's only done when there's a specific reason
reviewQuiz.explanation: Routine episiotomy is no longer recommended. Providers use it only when there's a specific reason.
